messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: parser / forgetting to declare stuff
parts:
Hi,

When you parse a .stan file that utilizes a vector that hasn't been
declared, you get an error like this

expression base type=UNKNOWN
too many index dimensions; require at most 0 found 1

I think a better error message would say "you didn't declare this
vector or you may have declared it to be a scalar but are using it in
a way that assumes it is a vector". Not sure what to do about the case
where the model utilizes a scalar that hasn't been declared, but it
would be nice to have a more informative error message in that case
too.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] parser / forgetting to declare stuff
parts:
Could you provide a Stan model that does this?

The compiler should catch undefined variables. What
I probably did was check for dimensionality match
even before I check for variable well-definedness.

There are three flavors of error:

data { }
derived data {
double y;
vector(10) z;

x[5] <- 2.0; // (1) unknown variable
y[5] <- 2.0; // (2) known variable, too many indices
z <- 2.0; // (3) mismatched LHS and RHS

y <- 2.0; // OK
z[5] <- 2.0; // OK
}

The check for whether a variable is unknown should happen
before the index test. The kind of message you saw is
intended for the "too many indices" and "too few indices"
cases. I should dump out the name of the variable, too.

I need to work on the error messages (it's on the to-do
for version 1), but I'm catching them the right way for now.
Here's what happens for the above:

(1) EXCEPTION. variable does not exist

(2) expression base type=double
too many index dimensions; require at most 0 found 1
too many index dimensions; require at most 0 found 1

EXCEPTION. parse error at file STDIN line 5 column 5
y[1] <- 2.0;
^-- here

(3) EXCEPTION. parse error at file STDIN line 5 column 5
z <- 2.0;
^-- here


- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: parser / forgetting to declare stuff
parts:
On 1/10/12 6:32 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> Can we evaluate the log posterior on iteration 0 with a higher level
> of scrutiny than subsequent iterations?

Warning: back to Stan-dev.

Yes, that would be easy. What do you want to scrutinize?

I'm guessing we're just going to have to bail if
it's ever -infinity or NaN. If we have a bad initial
init, we almost certainly won't be able to move into another
state at all. It's different after that, in that we can
just keep rejecting.

But we're also monitoring rejection rate, or some approximation
thereof, so we should catch a long string of rejections, too.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: parser / forgetting to declare stuff
parts:
I'd say check everything we can think of on iteration 0 and much less
for subsequent iterations. So for iteration 0,

-- Accessing vector / matrix elements all within range
-- Are all pointers non-null
-- Is every data point and parameter finite
-- All derivatives non-zero but finite
-- ...

Also, maybe we could try to extrapolate on iteration 0 whether the
consumption of time, RAM, etc. is going to be reasonable and print
that to stdout.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: parser / forgetting to declare stuff
parts:
Thanks for the suggestions.

Given the flexibility of the language, things
can still go wrong later, but most of the errors
will be in the first iteration, so we could be
more stringent. I tend to think like an all-or-nothing
computer scientist -- either I can guarantee it's
safe or not. And we can't really guarantee safety -- the
best we can do is check declared constraints.

The only way to get a null pointer is if a
parameter or derived parameter or local model
variable is used before it is assigned a value.

Positiveness of derivative is a good thing to
check everywhere. As you move around the space,
you can wind up in bad places if you don't have
the right constraints, etc.

I definitely want to profile with an expected
time-to-completion. The problem with that for Stan
is that there's a long adaptive burn-in/adaptation (of
step size) phase that's rather different than what
happens later. And the real big problem is that
the number of steps varies dramatically with step
size, so until we burn-in/adapt, it's hard to estimate
time until completion.

- Bob

Also, I think stan does not quite do Hessians yet, but when it does,
then checking that the Hessian is not too close to singular on
iteration 0 would be even better than checking whether the first
derivatives are non-zero.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: parser / forgetting to declare stuff
parts:
Hessians are expensive (stacked auto-dif) -- an N
dimensional Hessian requiring N gradients.

The idea's to use forward auto-dif for computing

d/dy[n] logp(y),

then using reverse mode on this to get the rows of
the Hessian,

grad d/dy[n] logp(y).

I started a forward auto-dif package, but it's definitely
not going to be ready for v1.

- Bob
